q: The European AI Office is administratively located in:
b: The Commission's DG CNECT (Communications Networks, Content and Technology)
explain: Established by Commission Decision of 24 January 2024, the AI Office sits within DG CNECT and provides Union-level AI expertise, GPAI enforcement and codes of practice.

q: The AI Act Scientific Panel of independent experts was formally established in June 2026 with:
a: Up to 60 independent experts on two-year renewable terms
b: 27 national ministers
explain: Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/454; panel launched 1 June 2026 — up to 60 experts, at least one per EU/EFTA/EEA state (max 3 per state). It advises the AI Office and can issue qualified alerts on GPAI systemic risk.

q: By its 2 August 2025 deadline, designation of national competent authorities under the AI Act was:
b: Widely missed — only a minority of Member States had designated both required authorities
explain: Implementation lags: by early 2026 only around 9 Member States had designated both market-surveillance and notifying authorities — context the exam may probe as 'state of implementation'.

q: The GPAI Code of Practice's three chapters are:
b: Transparency, Copyright, and Safety & Security
explain: Published 10 July 2025. Transparency and Copyright apply to all GPAI providers; Safety & Security only to providers of systemic-risk models (>10^25 FLOPs).

q: Full Commission enforcement powers over GPAI obligations (fines, requests for information, model access) apply from:
b: 2 August 2026, after a one-year grace period from the obligations' start
explain: GPAI obligations applied from 2 Aug 2025, but the AI Act gave the Commission enforcement tools a year later — from 2 Aug 2026.

q: The Digital Omnibus on AI (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744) entered into force in:
b: July 2026, following Council approval on 29 June 2026
explain: Published in the OJ on 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026. It defers Annex III high-risk to 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I to 2 Aug 2028, adds the NCII/CSAM prohibition, and introduces simplifications including the 'small mid-cap' category.

q: Besides the AI Act, the Digital Omnibus on AI also amended:
a: The GDPR and the ePrivacy Directive
b: The EASA Basic Regulation (2018/1139) and the Machinery Regulation (2023/1230)
explain: The Omnibus aligned sectoral product law (aviation, machinery) with the deferred AI high-risk timelines — it did not touch the GDPR, DSA or DMA.

q: The 'small mid-cap' (SMC) category introduced by the Digital Omnibus matters because:
a: SMCs are exempt from the AI Act entirely
b: It extends SME-style simplified documentation and compliance burdens to companies somewhat larger than SMEs
c: It creates a new tax bracket
explain: Part of the Commission's simplification agenda: proportionate obligations for small mid-caps alongside SMEs, e.g. simplified technical documentation.

q: The Data Act (Reg. (EU) 2023/2854) became applicable on:
b: 1 January 2024
explain: The Data Act applies from 12 Sept 2025: IoT/connected-product data access for users, business-to-business sharing terms, cloud switching. 'Data by design' duties for new products follow from 12 Sept 2026.

q: The Data Act chiefly regulates:
b: Access to and sharing of data generated by connected products and related services, plus cloud switching and unfair contractual terms
explain: It gives users of connected products rights over generated data, sets FRAND-style sharing conditions, and eases switching between data-processing services — complementing, not replacing, the GDPR.

q: The Data Governance Act (Reg. (EU) 2022/868) established:
b: Frameworks for re-use of protected public-sector data, notified data intermediation services, and data altruism organisations
explain: The DGA (applicable since Sept 2023) is the trust framework: public-sector data re-use, neutral data intermediaries, and altruistic data donation — infrastructure for the common European data spaces.

q: Common European data spaces are:
b: Sector-specific federated data-sharing ecosystems (health, mobility, energy, agriculture…) built on common governance and interoperability rules
c: Cloud regions operated by US providers
explain: The European data strategy's flagship: sectoral data spaces (with EHDS the first legislated one) to make data flow within trusted EU frameworks — key training-data context for AI policy.

q: The European Health Data Space Regulation (Reg. (EU) 2025/327):
b: Entered into force in March 2025, enabling primary use (patient access, cross-border) and secondary use of health data for research, with main secondary-use provisions applying around 2029
d: Replaces the GDPR for health data
explain: EHDS is the first sectoral data space in law: in force 26 March 2025, phased application (secondary-use core ~March 2029; some data categories 2031).

q: The DSA and the AI Act divide labour how?
a: They regulate the same thing twice
b: The DSA regulates online platforms/intermediaries (moderation, recommender transparency, VLOP systemic risk); the AI Act regulates AI systems themselves wherever deployed
c: The DSA is only for social media ads
d: The AI Act supersedes the DSA
explain: Platform duties vs product duties. A VLOP's recommender falls under DSA systemic-risk rules; the same company's AI system obligations come from the AI Act.

q: Under the DSA, 'VLOP' designation means:
b: A platform with over 45 million average monthly active EU users, subject to systemic-risk assessment, audits and data access for researchers
c: A platform with over 1 billion global users
explain: 45m ≈ 10% of the EU population. Around 17+ VLOPs designated; ChatGPT was designated as a Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE) — an AI-relevant DSA first.

q: The DMA regulates 'gatekeepers', which as of 2026 include:
b: Seven designated companies: Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Booking.com, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft
explain: The DMA imposes ex-ante do's and don'ts (interoperability, no self-preferencing, data-combination limits) on designated core platform services of these seven gatekeepers.

q: NIS2 (Directive (EU) 2022/2555) required Member State transposition by:
a: 17 October 2024 — a deadline many Member States missed, leading to infringement action and CJEU referrals in 2026
b: 2 August 2025
d: It is directly applicable and needs no transposition
explain: NIS2 is a directive (unlike the AI Act). Transposition was due 17 Oct 2024; in July 2026 the Commission referred several Member States to the CJEU for failure to transpose.

q: NIS2 applies to:
b: 'Essential' and 'important' entities in critical sectors (energy, transport, health, digital infrastructure…), imposing organisational cybersecurity risk management and incident reporting
explain: Organisation-level cybersecurity across 18 sectors with management accountability and 24h/72h incident reporting — complementary to product-level rules (AI Act Art 15, CRA).

q: The Cyber Resilience Act (Reg. (EU) 2024/2847) covers:
b: Cybersecurity requirements for products with digital elements across their lifecycle, with CE marking; main obligations fully applicable 11 December 2027
explain: CRA = product cybersecurity (secure-by-design, vulnerability handling, updates). In force 10 Dec 2024; reporting duties phase in 2026, full application 11 Dec 2027. Meeting CRA requirements supports AI Act Art 15 conformity.

q: The Digital Decade Policy Programme 2030 sets which target for ICT specialists in the EU?
b: 10 million
explain: 2030 targets: 20m ICT specialists (with gender convergence), 80% of adults with basic digital skills, 75% of EU companies using cloud/AI/big data, gigabit connectivity for all, 100% key public services online.

q: The Digital Decade target for enterprise AI uptake is:
b: 75% of EU companies using cloud, AI or big data by 2030
explain: The 75% cloud/AI/big-data uptake target is the business-digitalisation pillar; annual State of the Digital Decade reports track (and show gaps against) it.

q: The AI Continent Action Plan (April 2025) is built around:
b: Compute infrastructure (AI Factories and Gigafactories), data, skills, sectoral adoption and simplification — to make the EU a leading 'AI continent'
explain: Announced 9 April 2025: scaling EuroHPC-based AI Factories, up to 5 AI Gigafactories, data-union strategy, skills, and the Apply AI adoption push.

q: AI Factories are:
b: AI-optimised supercomputing hubs built around EuroHPC machines, giving startups, SMEs and researchers access to compute, data and talent services
d: Private US cloud regions in the EU
explain: 19+ AI Factories selected across Member States under EuroHPC JU — the EU's answer to compute access for its AI ecosystem; Gigafactories (~100k+ advanced AI chips) are the next scale step.

q: InvestAI aims to mobilise approximately:
b: €20 billion total
c: €200 billion for AI investment, including a ~€20 billion fund for AI gigafactories
explain: Announced at the February 2025 AI Action Summit in Paris: €200bn overall mobilisation with a €20bn public-private gigafactory facility; the EuroHPC gigafactory call followed in July 2026.

q: The Apply AI Strategy (October 2025) focuses on:
b: Accelerating AI adoption in strategic EU sectors and the public sector, with about €1 billion mobilised and an 'AI first' policy push
explain: COM(2025)724, presented 8 Oct 2025 alongside the AI in Science strategy: sectoral adoption (health, manufacturing, energy…), Apply AI Alliance, ~€1bn from existing programmes.

q: The EU's AI in Science strategy includes RAISE, which is:
a: A new tax on AI companies
b: A (pilot) virtual European institute pooling resources to attract and support AI talent in science
explain: RAISE (Resource for AI Science in Europe) pilots pooling compute/data/talent for AI-driven research, funded via Horizon Europe — part of the Oct 2025 strategy package.

q: The Coordinated Plan on AI is:
b: A joint Commission-Member States framework (2018, revised 2021) aligning national AI strategies and investment, targeting €20bn/year of AI investment this decade
explain: Soft-coordination instrument predating the AI Act; most Member States now have national AI strategies under it. Progress is reviewed jointly with the OECD.

q: EuroHPC Joint Undertaking is:
b: The EU body pooling EU and national funding to procure and operate world-class supercomputers — now also mandated to host AI Factories and Gigafactories
explain: EuroHPC JU (machines like LUMI, Leonardo, JUPITER — the EU's first exascale system) had its mandate extended in 2026 to the AI gigafactory programme.

q: The AI Act's national regulatory sandboxes are intended primarily to:
b: Let providers, especially SMEs and startups, develop and test innovative AI under regulatory supervision before market placement
explain: Art 57: at least one sandbox per Member State by 2 Aug 2026, with priority SME access — the innovation-support counterweight to the Act's obligations.

q: Which body issues opinions and coordinates consistent AI Act application across Member States?
b: ENISA
explain: The AI Board (one representative per Member State, Art 65) coordinates national implementation and advises the Commission — with the Advisory Forum providing stakeholder input.

q: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (2024) differs from the AI Act in that it:
a: Regulates products for the internal market
b: Is an international human-rights treaty on AI open to non-European states, setting principles rather than product-conformity rules
explain: The CoE Convention (signed by the EU, US, UK among others) is rights-principles-based international law; the AI Act is detailed internal-market product regulation.

q: The GDPR's role in the EU AI landscape is best summarised as:
b: The horizontal personal-data layer: lawful basis, purpose limitation, data-subject rights and DPIAs apply to AI training and use whenever personal data is processed
explain: EDPB opinions address AI-model training and lawful basis; the AI Act repeatedly defers to the GDPR — exam questions like testing that both apply cumulatively.

q: Standardisation supporting the AI Act is led by:
b: CEN and CENELEC (notably JTC 21) under a Commission standardisation request, producing harmonised European standards that give presumption of conformity
explain: European harmonised standards (hENs), once cited in the OJ, trigger the Art 40 presumption of conformity — why the delayed JTC 21 work programme matters to the whole timeline.

q: ENISA is:
b: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity — supporting NIS2 implementation, certification schemes and cyber preparedness
explain: ENISA anchors the cybersecurity side (NIS2, EU cybersecurity certification under the Cybersecurity Act) — adjacent to, but distinct from, AI Act governance.

q: The EU's approach to general-purpose AI risk is internationally distinctive because it:
b: Imposes binding legal obligations on GPAI providers (transparency, copyright, systemic-risk duties) where most jurisdictions rely on voluntary commitments
explain: Chapter V is the first binding GPAI regime; the US executive-order/voluntary approach and UK safety-institute model contrast with it — a classic comparative-policy question.

q: 'Digital sovereignty' / 'strategic autonomy' in EU AI policy refers to:
b: Reducing critical dependencies (chips, cloud, foundation models) and building EU capacity — compute, data, talent — while remaining open
explain: The motivation behind the Chips Act, EuroHPC/AI Factories, InvestAI and data-space policy: capacity and resilience, not isolation.

q: The European Chips Act aims to:
b: Double the EU's share of global semiconductor production toward 20% by 2030 through public-private investment and fab support
explain: Semiconductors are the compute substrate of AI policy; the Chips Act (2023) is the supply-side complement to AI Factories and Gigafactories.

q: Under the AI Act, deepfake labelling obligations (Art 50) sit in EU disinformation policy alongside:
b: The DSA's systemic-risk duties for VLOPs and the (strengthened) Code of Practice/Conduct on Disinformation
explain: Synthetic-content transparency (AI Act) + platform risk mitigation (DSA) + the disinformation code integrated into the DSA co-regulatory framework — the layered EU answer to AI-driven disinformation.

q: The 'Brussels effect' in AI policy describes:
b: EU rules becoming de facto global standards as multinational providers align worldwide products with the strictest major market
explain: As with the GDPR, the AI Act's extraterritorial reach and market size push global compliance alignment — a standard policy-analysis concept the essay or MCQ can invoke.

q: AI literacy policy in the EU (AI Act Art 4 plus skills programmes) is supported financially mainly by:
b: Digital Europe Programme, Horizon Europe and related instruments funding digital skills, research and deployment
explain: DIGITAL (deployment, skills, AI testing facilities) and Horizon Europe (research) are the twin funding arms behind the Digital Decade skills targets.

q: Which statement about the AI Act's essay-worthy 'innovation vs regulation' debate is factually accurate as of 2026?
a: The EU abandoned the AI Act
b: The Commission pursued simplification (Digital Omnibus deferrals, SME/SMC relief) while keeping prohibitions and transparency on schedule — responding to competitiveness critiques like the Draghi report
explain: The 2026 policy story: burden-reduction and deadline deferral for high-risk compliance, paired with unchanged fundamentals — framed by the Draghi competitiveness report's critique of regulatory load.

q: The EDPS's AI-related role includes:
b: Supervising EU institutions' own compliance — including acting as their market surveillance authority under the AI Act and imposing fines under Art 100
explain: The EDPS wears two hats: data-protection supervisor of EU institutions and their AI Act surveillance authority — while national authorities and the AI Office cover everyone else.

q: 'High-impact' international AI safety cooperation the EU participates in includes:
b: AI safety summits/network of safety institutes, the G7 Hiroshima Process code of conduct, and OECD AI work
explain: The AI Office represents the EU in the international safety-institute network; the Hiroshima Process produced the G7 voluntary code for advanced AI developers; the OECD hosts definitions and metrics.

q: Open-source AI in EU policy is treated as:
b: Favoured with targeted exemptions (AI Act GPAI documentation relief unless systemic-risk) and seen as an ecosystem asset, though obligations return for systemic-risk models
explain: The Act balances openness benefits against frontier-risk: open-weight models get documentation relief but keep copyright/training-summary duties, and lose relief entirely at systemic-risk scale.

q: Which pairing of instrument → primary object is correct?
a: DGA → platform moderation; DSA → data intermediaries
b: DMA → gatekeeper contestability; NIS2 → organisational cybersecurity; CRA → product cybersecurity; Data Act → connected-product data access
c: CRA → AI conformity; AI Act → chip subsidies
explain: The acquis map in one line — the exam's favourite 'which law does what' pattern. DGA = data-sharing trust framework; DSA = platform duties.

q: An EU agency wants to deploy a high-risk AI system for visa application triage. Before first use it must, among other things:
b: Complete a FRIA (Art 27), ensure registration checks, and operate under EDPS supervision as its surveillance authority
explain: Public bodies deploying Annex III systems carry the FRIA duty; for EU institutions the EDPS supervises. Migration/border is Annex III area 7 — a realistic institutional scenario.

q: The AI Office's five units cover which portfolio areas?
b: Excellence in AI & Robotics; Regulation & Compliance; AI Safety; AI Innovation & Policy Coordination; AI for Societal Good
explain: The Office combines enforcement (Regulation & Compliance, AI Safety) with promotion (Excellence, Innovation, Societal Good) — mirroring the EU's twin-track 'trustworthy AI + competitiveness' strategy.

q: Which is TRUE about AI Act penalties and the GPAI Code of Practice?
a: Signing the Code is legally mandatory
b: Signing is voluntary; signatories get a recognised route to demonstrate compliance and reduced administrative scrutiny, while non-signatories must prove compliance by other means
d: The Code replaces the Act for signatories
explain: The Commission confirmed the Code as an adequate voluntary compliance tool (Aug 2025); some major providers signed, others (e.g. Meta) declined — both paths remain legal.

q: The EU's public-sector interoperability framework for digital government is anchored by:
b: The Data Act
explain: The Interoperable Europe Act (2024) sets mandatory interoperability assessments and the Interoperable Europe Board for cross-border digital public services — the GovTech layer AI-in-government sits on.

q: eIDAS 2.0 (Reg. (EU) 2024/1183) introduced:
b: The European Digital Identity Wallet, to be offered by every Member State, for cross-border identification and credential sharing
explain: EUDI Wallets (due to citizens by end-2026) underpin trusted digital transactions — identity infrastructure relevant to AI-era authentication and age verification debates.

q: The EU's 2026 CJEU referrals of several Member States (Ireland, Spain, France, Netherlands) concerned failure to transpose:
b: NIS2
explain: Trap alignment: the AI Act is a regulation (no transposition needed); NIS2 is a directive and its missed transposition triggered the July 2026 referrals.

q: Which EU institution formally adopts EPSO-relevant AI legislation like the AI Act?
b: The European Parliament and the Council, as co-legislators under the ordinary legislative procedure, on a Commission proposal
explain: Ordinary legislative procedure: Commission proposes, Parliament and Council co-decide. The Commission then adopts delegated/implementing acts (e.g. Annex III updates, Scientific Panel rules).

q: The Commission may amend Annex III (high-risk use cases) via:
a: A new full regulation each time
b: Delegated acts, adding or modifying use cases within the Act's defined areas based on risk evidence
explain: Art 7 empowers delegated acts to keep the high-risk list current — the mechanism that makes the Act adaptive without reopening the legislative procedure.

q: 'AI factories antennas' and gigafactory site selection in 2026 are run under:
b: EuroHPC JU calls, following its mandate extension to AI infrastructure and the official gigafactory call of July 2026
explain: The EuroHPC gigafactory call (30 July 2026) operationalises InvestAI: sites hosting ~100k+ advanced AI processors for training frontier-scale models in the EU.

q: The EU's position on general-purpose AI and copyright currently rests on:
b: The DSM Directive's TDM exceptions (Arts 3-4) plus AI Act Art 53 duties (copyright policy, training-content summary) — with court cases and a possible review ongoing
c: Full exemption of AI training from copyright
explain: No dedicated AI-copyright instrument exists; the TDM opt-out + transparency duties carry the load while litigation and policy review continue — an active, examinable policy frontier.

q: Which statement about AI and EU competition policy is accurate?
b: The Commission scrutinises AI partnerships and acquisitions (e.g. big-tech/model-lab alliances) under merger and antitrust tools, and the DMA can reach AI services integrated into gatekeeper platforms
c: AI companies are exempt from merger control
d: Only national authorities act on AI
explain: Competition policy is the fourth leg of EU AI governance: reviewing partnerships without formal mergers, cloud-compute dependencies, and DMA coverage as AI integrates into core platform services.

q: The 'twin transition' in EU policy language couples:
a: Digital and green transformations, with AI expected to contribute to both competitiveness and sustainability goals
b: Public and private sectors
explain: Digital + green is the standing Commission frame; AI's energy footprint vs its optimisation potential (energy grids, materials) is a common essay/MCQ angle.

q: Which funding programme most directly finances deployment-oriented AI capacity (testing facilities, skills, data spaces)?
b: The Digital Europe Programme (DIGITAL)
explain: DIGITAL funds AI testing and experimentation facilities, EDIHs, skills and data spaces; Horizon Europe covers research; both feed the AI Continent agenda.

q: European Digital Innovation Hubs (EDIHs) are:
b: A network of one-stop shops helping SMEs and public administrations test and adopt digital and AI technologies, co-funded by DIGITAL
explain: 200+ EDIHs provide test-before-invest, skills and financing guidance — the retail layer of EU AI adoption policy, complementing AI Factories' compute layer.

q: As of late 2026, the accurate one-line summary of AI Act implementation status is:
b: Prohibitions, GPAI rules, governance and transparency apply; high-risk obligations are deferred (Annex III to Dec 2027, Annex I to Aug 2028) by the Digital Omnibus; standards and national authority designations are still catching up
explain: The status-quo snapshot an examiner would expect a candidate to hold in September 2026 — staged application plus simplification, not retreat.
